interviewQuestions.question: Why does random forest rarely overfit even with very deep, individually overfitting trees?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd separate the bias/variance profile of a single tree from that of the ensemble, because random forest's trick isn't reducing each tree's individual variance — it's letting many high-variance trees cancel each other out. A deep, unconstrained tree genuinely has low bias and very high variance: it fits training noise almost perfectly, memorizing quirks specific to the exact rows it saw. Random forest doesn't fix that per-tree behavior at all — each individual tree, examined alone, would still overfit badly on its own.

What makes the ensemble safe is that averaging N models whose errors are largely independent drives the averaged variance toward roughly the per-model variance divided by N, since independent errors partially cancel rather than compounding. Each tree trains on a different bootstrap sample and, in random forest specifically, considers only a random subset of features per split — both sources of randomness push different trees toward overfitting to *different* specific noise patterns. Since the noise each tree memorizes tends to differ tree to tree, those overfitting mistakes point in largely uncorrelated directions and wash out when votes are averaged, while the genuine signal every tree is still roughly tracking survives and reinforces itself.

The crucial caveat, which is why feature-subsampling exists at all: bagging alone still lets a few dominant features control the top split of nearly every tree, making trees more correlated than pure bootstrap randomness suggests — correlated errors don't cancel as well as independent ones. Random forest's feature-subsampling step specifically breaks that dominance, decorrelating trees further and making the variance-cancellation argument hold more strongly.

**Testing:** whether you distinguish a single tree's bias/variance from the ensemble's, and can explain averaging as cancellation of largely-independent errors, contingent on the trees actually being decorrelated — not just "averaging fixes overfitting" as an unexplained rule.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Depth is safe inside an ensemble

interviewQuestions.question: What's out-of-bag error, and why is it a genuinely valid substitute for a held-out validation set rather than just a cheap trick?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Each tree in a random forest trains on a bootstrap sample — drawn with replacement from the full training set, the same size as the original — and because sampling with replacement leaves some rows unpicked, roughly 37% of the original rows are excluded from any given tree's training sample purely as a mathematical consequence of the sampling process (the probability a specific row is never drawn across N draws with replacement converges to 1/e ≈ 0.37 as N grows). Those excluded rows are "out-of-bag" for that specific tree — the tree genuinely never saw them during training, in exactly the same sense a held-out validation set is never seen during training.

For any given training row, some subset of the forest's trees excluded it (roughly a third of all trees, on average) while the rest included it. To compute the OOB prediction for that row, you use only the trees that excluded it — a genuinely honest out-of-sample prediction for that specific row, made by models that never trained on it — and compare that prediction to the true label. Averaging this check across every row in the training set gives the OOB error, and this is legitimately equivalent in spirit to a held-out validation check, not an approximation of one, because for every single row the prediction really did come from models with zero exposure to it.

The practical payoff: you get a validation-quality generalization estimate without sacrificing any training data to a held-out split — every row is used both to help train roughly two-thirds of the forest and to validate against the remaining third, essentially getting the benefit of cross-validation as a byproduct of how bagging already works, at no extra computational or data cost.

**Testing:** whether you can justify why OOB error is a genuinely valid held-out estimate (each excluded row really is unseen by the trees used to score it), not just describe the mechanic without explaining why it's trustworthy.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why OOB error is a genuine validation signal

interviewQuestions.question: Your team ranks features by built-in Gini importance and a customer ID field (thousands of distinct values) shows up as highly important, more so than a genuinely predictive but low-cardinality feature. What's going on?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
This is a well-known artifact of how Gini-based feature importance is computed, and it specifically favors high-cardinality features regardless of whether they're genuinely predictive — treating the ranking as ground truth here would be a real mistake. A feature with many distinct values (like a customer ID with thousands of unique entries) offers the tree-building algorithm many more candidate split points to try than a low-cardinality feature (like a binary flag with only one possible split point). More candidate splits means more chances that at least one of them happens to reduce impurity by pure chance alone, purely from having more attempts — not because the feature carries genuine signal. Across many trees in a forest, this chance-driven impurity reduction accumulates into an importance score that looks substantial, even for a feature with literally no real relationship to the target, like a customer ID that's essentially a random identifier.

This is a structural bias in the built-in importance metric, not something specific to this dataset — it will show up whenever features of very different cardinality are compared using Gini or entropy-based importance, and it gets worse the larger the cardinality gap.

The fix is switching to permutation importance instead: for each feature, randomly shuffle its values (breaking any real relationship it has to the target) and measure how much the model's accuracy on held-out (or OOB) data drops as a result. A feature with no genuine predictive power will show little to no accuracy drop when shuffled, regardless of its cardinality, because permutation importance measures actual predictive contribution rather than counting split opportunities. I'd recompute the ranking with permutation importance before trusting any conclusion about which features actually matter, especially before removing the low-cardinality feature that Gini importance is currently underrating.

**Testing:** whether you can explain the actual mechanism behind the cardinality bias (more split points, more chance-driven impurity reduction), not just recite "Gini importance is biased toward high-cardinality features."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Diagnosing cardinality bias in feature importance
